label: Verve
rationale: Bill Evans alone, three times over: the first serious jazz record built on multi-tracked improvisation, and the one that made the technique an artistic argument rather than a gimmick — Evans wrote a defense into the liner notes because he knew it would be called one (S1). Recorded February 6 and 9 and (per the standard discographies) May 20, 1963 at Webster Hall, New York, on Glenn Gould's Steinway CD 318, produced by Creed Taylor, engineered by Ray Hall (S1, S3, S4, S5). The consensus signals are explicit and unusually varied: it won the 1964 Grammy for Best Jazz Instrumental Album, Individual or Group — Evans's first Grammy — was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2000, and drew five stars from DownBeat in 1963, 4.5 from AllMusic (Nastos), 4.5 from the Penguin Guide and 3.5 from All About Jazz (S1). Lineage is the stronger case: everything Evans did afterward with overdubbing (Further Conversations, 1967; New Conversations, 1978) descends from it, Terry Riley cited it, Fred Hersch and Jean-Yves Thibaudet built tributes on it, and the model of a pianist in dialogue with himself runs straight through the solo-piano tradition the canon already holds — Evans's Alone (1970) and Monk's Solo Monk are both already in (S1). The programme is not filler: three Monk pieces against five standards, with 'N.Y.C.'s No Lark' written for Sonny Clark the month Clark died, and the Spartacus love theme singled out by Evans's biographers as the record's peak (S1).

personnel.name: Bill Evans
personnel.notes: Solo, multi-tracked: three overdubbed piano parts on every piece except 'Blue Monk', which uses two (S1, S4). Played Glenn Gould's Steinway CD 318 (S1, S5).

cover_art.notes: Front cover served by Cover Art Archive for this release group.

personnel_record.notes: Session distribution per S3: February 6 — 'N.Y.C.'s No Lark'; February 9 — ''Round Midnight', 'How About You?', 'Stella by Starlight', 'Hey There', 'Just You, Just Me' (plus 'A Sleepin' Bee', added on CD reissues); May 20 — 'Love Theme from Spartacus', 'Blue Monk'. 'Bemsha Swing' is dated only to February 1963 by S3 (catalogued via The Best of Bill Evans) and carries a null session_date here rather than a guessed day. UNRESOLVED CONFLICT — third session date: S3 and S1 give 1963-05-20 for the Spartacus/Blue Monk date (master numbers 63VK488-489), while S4 and S5 (Creed Taylor session account and Gene Lees' liner-note reconstruction) place the third date on February 20, 1963; Lees' notes themselves say only 'January and February 1963'. The 1963-05-20 date is carried in recording_dates and the venue (Webster Hall) is agreed by every source, so the site claim is obs; the date should be read as disputed. Engineer Ray Hall and director of engineering Val Valentin per S4 and S5; AllMusic credits do not list production roles for this title, so production is carried as obs on the session accounts.

ballot.case_for: Evans makes overdubbing a substantive extension of post-bebop improvisation: layered performances expose his harmonic thinking and contrapuntal imagination in a defining statement he subsequently revisited on Further Conversations and New Conversations (S1, S4). Recognition is unusually broad: the dossier reports a 1964 Grammy, Grammy Hall of Fame induction, five stars from DownBeat, and 4.5 stars from both Penguin and AllMusic, although most of these claims are collected through S1. The original program's Monk interpretations, standards, 'N.Y.C.'s No Lark,' and 'Love Theme from Spartacus' give the experiment expressive substance beyond its recording method (S1, S3).
ballot.case_against: Overdubbing replaces reciprocal ensemble interaction with improvisation against fixed performances; its dense piano counterpoint can obscure the space, swing, and immediacy that make Evans's trio and unaccompanied work compelling introductions. The historical innovation therefore does not guarantee discovery value for a listener encountering the album cold. Evidence for broad recognition is stronger than the dossier's independently documented influence claims: awards, ratings, and later-musician connections rely heavily on S1, and the claim of historical priority needs firmer sourcing. The dossier also conflates the expanded edition with the original eight-track LP and retains an unresolved February-versus-May third-session date conflict (S1, S3–S6).
ballot.disagreement: Both references agree on consensus_core and strong, with no scope dispute. They differ in the weight given to reservations: the first treats independent sourcing and edition accuracy as substantive qualifications and calls discovery value plausible, while the second finds discovery value exceptional and treats the aesthetic objections as insufficient to challenge canonical standing.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John give this strong-priority consideration as a consensus-core candidate, with the original LP distinguished from the expanded edition and the sourcing and session-date caveats retained.
